note: Curated featured stories (bounded research batches; every story cites sources).

items.name: Sun
items.hook: The star that powers nearly all life on Earth.
items.story: The Sun holds about 99.86% of all the mass in the Solar System and is about 109 times wider than Earth. Every second its core fuses roughly 600 billion kilograms of hydrogen into helium. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.

items.name: Proxima Centauri
items.hook: Our closest stellar neighbor, a tiny flaring red dwarf.
items.story: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to Earth after the Sun, just 4.25 light-years away, yet too faint to see without a telescope. This small red dwarf is a flare star that randomly brightens dramatically. It has at least two known planets, including Proxima b, which circles the star every 11.2 days.

items.name: Alpha Centauri
items.hook: A three-star system right next door to the Sun.
items.story: Alpha Centauri is a system of three stars: two Sun-like stars, Rigil Kentaurus and Toliman, plus the red dwarf Proxima Centauri. The bright pair look like one star, the third-brightest in the night sky. The pair circle each other every 79 years, at times as far apart as Pluto is from the Sun.

items.name: Barnard's Star
items.hook: The closest single star in the northern sky.
items.story: At 5.96 light-years away, Barnard's Star is the closest star in the northern celestial hemisphere, but it is too dim to see with the naked eye. For decades, claims of planets here fell apart, until two teams found four small, close-orbiting planets in 2024 and 2025.

items.name: Sirius
items.hook: The brightest star in the night sky has a hidden partner.
items.story: Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky, partly because it is only 8.6 light-years away. It is actually two stars: a bright white star and a faint white dwarf companion, Sirius B, which orbit each other every 50 years. Around the year 66,270, Sirius will become the southern pole star.

items.name: Vega
items.hook: Once the North Star, and it will be again.
items.story: Vega was the first star other than the Sun to have its picture and its spectrum photographed. It is just 25 light-years away and served as a standard for measuring star brightness. Thanks to Earth's slow wobble, Vega was the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE and will be again around the year 13,724.

items.name: Polaris
items.hook: The North Star is really three stars in one.
items.story: Polaris sits less than one degree from the north celestial pole, which makes it useful for navigation. It looks like one point of light, but it is a triple star system. Its main star is the closest Cepheid variable, a type of pulsating star astronomers use to measure cosmic distances.

items.name: Betelgeuse
items.hook: A giant red star expected to explode as a supernova.
items.story: Betelgeuse, Orion's red shoulder, is so huge that if it replaced the Sun its surface would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. It is expected to explode as a supernova, likely within 100,000 years. When it does, it will shine about as bright as a half-Moon for over three months.

items.name: Rigel
items.hook: Orion's blazing blue-white supergiant, thousands of times brighter than the Sun.
items.story: Rigel is a blue supergiant in Orion, tens of thousands of times more luminous than the Sun and about 850 light-years away. What looks like one star is a system of at least four. Only seven to nine million years old, Rigel has already burned through its core hydrogen and will likely end as a supernova.

items.name: Arcturus
items.hook: An aging red giant and the north's brightest star.
items.story: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern half of the sky, about 36.7 light-years away. It is roughly as massive as the Sun, but at around 7.1 billion years old it has run out of core hydrogen and swollen to about 25 times the Sun's size, and is about 170 times as luminous.

items.name: Antares
items.hook: The red heart of the Scorpion, with a hidden companion.
items.story: Antares, the "heart of the scorpion," is a red supergiant so large that, placed at the Sun's position, it would reach into the asteroid belt. About 550 light-years away, it looks like one reddish star, but it actually has a fainter, hot companion star.

items.name: Deneb
items.hook: A distant supergiant that still shines brightly across thousands of light-years.
items.story: Deneb is a blue supergiant that marks one corner of the Summer Triangle and the head of the Northern Cross. It may be up to 196,000 times as luminous as the Sun. Its distance is uncertain, between 1,400 and 2,600 light-years; if the farther value is right, it is the most distant star this bright in our sky.

items.name: Tau Ceti
items.hook: A nearby Sun-like star and a favorite target for SETI.
items.story: Tau Ceti is the closest single G-type star, the same type as the Sun, just under 12 light-years away and visible to the naked eye. It is surrounded by more than ten times as much dust as our Solar System. Its stability and Sun-like nature make it a regular target in the search for alien intelligence.

items.name: TRAPPIST-1
items.hook: A tiny star with seven Earth-sized worlds.
items.story: TRAPPIST-1 is a cool red dwarf only slightly larger than Jupiter, about 40 light-years away. It hosts seven rocky planets, each orbiting in 1.5 to 19 days. Up to four of them lie at distances where temperatures may allow liquid water and all seven pass in front of the star as seen from Earth.

items.name: 61 Cygni
items.hook: The first star whose distance was ever measured.
items.story: 61 Cygni is a pair of orange dwarf stars that orbit each other about every 659 years. In 1838, Friedrich Bessel used it to make the first distance measurement to any star besides the Sun, finding about 10.4 light-years, close to the true 11.4. It moves across the sky faster than any other naked-eye star.

items.name: Pleiades
items.hook: The Seven Sisters: the most obvious star cluster in the sky.
items.story: About 444 light-years away, the Pleiades hold over 1,000 young stars, and six or seven are easy to see without a telescope. Its blue haze isn't leftover birth material; the cluster is passing through a dusty patch of space. In Japan it is called Subaru.

items.name: Hyades
items.hook: The nearest open cluster, about 153 light-years away.
items.story: The Hyades is the closest open cluster to the Sun, roughly 625 million years old. Bright Aldebaran looks like part of it but is actually much closer to us, at 65 light-years. Precise distances to the Hyades help astronomers calibrate the cosmic distance ladder.

items.name: Beehive Cluster (Praesepe)
items.hook: Galileo turned a fuzzy glow into 40 stars.
items.story: This cluster in Cancer lies about 610 light-years away and is around 600 to 700 million years old. In 1609 Galileo's telescope resolved it into 40 stars. In 2012 astronomers found two hot Jupiters here, the first planets found around Sun-like stars in star clusters.

items.name: Orion Nebula
items.hook: A star nursery you can see with your eyes.
items.story: Visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword, this nebula is about 1,270 light-years away and is the closest region of massive star formation to Earth. Hubble has spotted more than 150 protoplanetary disks here, which may be young solar systems still forming.

items.name: Crab Nebula
items.hook: Wreckage of a star that exploded in 1054.
items.story: The Crab Nebula is what remains of a bright supernova seen in AD 1054 and recorded by Chinese astronomers. At its heart is the Crab Pulsar, a neutron star that spins about 30 times every second. It lies roughly 6,500 light-years away.

items.name: Ring Nebula
items.hook: A dying star's glowing smoke ring.
items.story: About 2,570 light-years away in Lyra, this ring of glowing gas was blown off by a star near the end of its life. What's left at the center is a white dwarf. Charles Messier found it in 1779.

items.name: Dumbbell Nebula
items.hook: The first planetary nebula ever discovered.
items.story: Charles Messier discovered this cloud in Vulpecula in 1764, making it the first planetary nebula known. It lies about 1,360 light-years away, and its expanding gas suggests an age of roughly 9,800 years. A white dwarf at the center lights it up.

items.name: Eagle Nebula
items.hook: Home of Hubble's famous Pillars of Creation.
items.story: About 5,700 light-years away in Serpens, the Eagle Nebula holds a young star cluster and several active star-forming regions. In 1995 Hubble photographed its towering gas columns, now known as the Pillars of Creation, where new stars are forming.
items.type: Emission nebula (H II region) with open cluster

items.name: Lagoon Nebula
items.hook: A giant star-forming cloud faintly visible without a telescope.
items.story: This giant glowing cloud in Sagittarius is about 4,100 light-years away and spans about 110 by 50 light-years. It is one of only two star-forming nebulae faintly visible to the naked eye from mid-northern latitudes. Its central Hourglass region shows signs of stars being born.

items.name: Hercules Globular Cluster
items.hook: Humanity sent a radio message here in 1974.
items.story: Hundreds of thousands of stars crowd into this ball about 24,000 light-years away. Edmond Halley discovered it in 1714. In 1974, the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a coded message about humans, DNA, and Earth's location toward it.

items.name: Omega Centauri
items.hook: The Milky Way's biggest globular cluster, maybe a galaxy's core.
items.story: With about 10 million stars, Omega Centauri is the largest and most massive known globular cluster in the Milky Way. Ptolemy listed it as a single star. It may be the core of a dwarf galaxy swallowed by our galaxy, and a 2024 study reported possible evidence of a central black hole.

items.name: Messier 4 (Spider Globular Cluster)
items.hook: The closest globular cluster, hiding some of the galaxy's oldest stars.
items.story: About 6,000 light-years away near Antares, M4 is the closest globular cluster to the Solar System. Some of its white dwarfs are among the oldest known stars in our galaxy. It also hosts a pulsar system with a planet about 2.5 times Jupiter's mass.

items.name: Wild Duck Cluster
items.hook: A packed cluster shaped like a flock of flying ducks.
items.story: This cluster in Scutum, about 6,100 light-years away, is one of the richest and most compact open clusters known. Its brightest stars form a triangle that resembles a flying flock of ducks, which gives it its name. It is roughly 316 million years old.

items.name: Trifid Nebula
items.hook: Three kinds of nebula in one, split into three lobes.
items.story: About 4,100 light-years away in Sagittarius, the Trifid mixes a pink emission nebula, a blue reflection nebula, and dark dust lanes that split it into three lobes. It is a stellar nursery with about 3,100 young stars.

items.name: Andromeda Galaxy
items.hook: A whole other galaxy you can see with your eyes.
items.story: Unlike everything else here, Andromeda lies outside the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away, and holds roughly a trillion stars. It is visible to the naked eye on dark nights. It may one day collide with our galaxy, though newer Gaia-based studies make a merger look less likely.
items.type: Barred spiral galaxy (outside the Milky Way)
